newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: EA-Generali tops up CA offer as deadline looms.
newsitem.headline: EA-Generali tops up CA offer as deadline looms.

text.p: An international group of bidders for Austrian selloff candidate Creditanstalt on Wednesday raised its bid for the country's flagship bank, but its chances of success appeared increasingly slim.

The group, led by Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali, said it had decided to improve its previous offer of 13.8 billion schillings ($1.25 billion) for most of the state's 70 percent voting stake in the bank, but gave no further details.
"We have decided to improve our offer," EA-Generali chief executive Dietrich Karner told a news conference.
The consortium, an assortment of financial and industrial interests, is up against a rival bid from Bank Austria which has offered 16.8 billion schillings to take control of its main competitor.
Karner said it had not been the group's aim to outbid Bank Austria.
"It was not our goal to outdo Bank Austria, we were led by purely economic considerations," he said.

The politically-charged debate over who will get the prize has driven a wedge between Austria's uneasy coalition government partners. The dominant Social Democrats favour Bank Austria, while their junior coalition partner, the conservative People's Party, supports the EA-Generali led group.
A senior source close to the consortium said late on Wednesday even that if the group managed to match Bank Austria's bid, its chances of taking over Creditanstalt had all but waned.
"No chance," the source told Reuters. "We won't make it, even if we bid (just a little less) then Bank Austria."

If the consortium fails to outbid Bank Austria, the Social Democrats have left little doubt that a merger of the country's two top banks is on the cards, raising the spectre of a major shakeup in Austria's overcrowded banking system.
"A decision must be made ... for the best bidder and the highest offer. We're committed to that," Chancellor and Social Democratic Party chief Franz Vranitzky said.

Bank Austria's supervisory board was scheduled to convene at a special meeting on Thursday to review its own bid, one day before Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima's final deadline for adjusted offers runs out.

The debate over what has become Europe's longest-running privatisation battle plunged into increasingly murky waters on Wednesday with leaders of Austria's creaky government coalition publicly exchanging jibes over the hotly-contested sell-off.
Vranitzky said his party would not be bullied into a decision by the People's Party.

The conservatives, who fear losing control of Creditanstalt to "socialist"-controlled Bank Austria, have called a special session of parliament on Tuesday to discuss the sale. Senior members of both parties will meet in emergency talks on Monday.

Bank Austria is effectively controlled by the Social Democratic City of Vienna council through its Anteilsverwaltung Zentralsparkasse, which guarantees the bank's liabilities and has thus ensured Bank Austria's AAA rating.

Schuessel's attempt to appease his angry coalition partner by suggesting that Bank Austria might buy half of the state's Creditanstalt stake with the rest being floated on the stock exchange was flatly rejected by Vranitzky.
"This is a bad option...the law dictates that we sell to the highest bidder," the chancellor said. ($1=11.05 Schilling)
